judge_reasoning: The case Lighting World, Inc. v. Birchwood Lighting, Inc., 382 F.3d 1354 (Fed. Cir. 2004) is confirmed as a real Federal Circuit decision from September 3, 2004, available on Justia, Google Scholar, OpenJurist, FindLaw, and Leagle. All citation elements match exactly.

Multiple authoritative legal sources (Quimbee, Harvard Law Review, Wikipedia, SCOTUSblog) confirm this is a genuine U.S. Supreme Court per curiam decision reported at 140 S. Ct. 1525, decided April 27, 2020. The case name, reporter citation, and year all match exactly.

35 U.S.C. § 112(f) is a real and well-established provision of the United States Code (Title 35 - Patents), introduced by the America Invents Act to replace the former § 112 ¶ 6, governing means-plus-function claims in patent law. Multiple authoritative sources (govinfo.gov, USPTO documents) confirm its existence and content.

The case exists at exactly 792 F.3d 1339 (Fed. Cir. 2015), a landmark 2015 en banc Federal Circuit decision on means-plus-function claims. The only error is the defendant name: the actual style is 'Williamson v. Citrix Online, LLC,' not 'Citrix Systems, Inc.' This minor entity-name variation does not change which case is cited, as the reporter citation unambiguously identifies the real decision.

FindLaw's D.C. Circuit database returns a case titled exactly 'National Association of Manufacturers v. Department of Labor' and the search summary describes it as a D.C. Circuit EAJA attorney-fees decision, consistent with all cited attributes. The specific volume/page (801 F.3d 1298) could not be directly confirmed due to a 403 error on the case page, but no contradictory evidence was found.

The reporter citation 927 F.3d 1230 (Fed. Cir. 2019) is occupied by Mayne Pharma International Pty. Ltd. v. Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp., 927 F.3d 1232 (Fed. Cir. 2019), a patent/IPR case unrelated to MedDevice Partners or Abbott Laboratories. No legal database (CourtListener, Justia, Google Scholar) returns any result for 'MedDevice Partners LLC' as a party in any Federal Circuit case, and the party name itself appears to be a fabricated entity.

The paper exists at arXiv:1212.1603 with an exact title match and first author Daniel Petersson, submitted December 2012. The citation omits co-author Johan Löfberg, but this is a metadata error that does not prevent identification of the real work.

The Michigan Law Review Volume 119, Issue 8 (June 2021) was located and its full table of contents confirmed. That issue contains four articles on entirely unrelated topics, none by Zelik and none touching the Second Amendment, mootness, or ripeness. No trace of a Zelik article on this subject was found in any academic database, SSRN, or Google Scholar search.

The case Zampierollo-Rheinfeldt v. Ingersoll-Rand de Puerto Rico, Inc., No. 20-1356 (1st Cir. 2021) is confirmed real by multiple legal databases (Justia, FindLaw, UniCourt), with matching court and year. The reporter citation 999 F.3d 37 is plausible for a May 2021 First Circuit decision, and no evidence contradicts the page number, though it could not be independently confirmed from open-web sources.

The DOI 10.2139/ssrn.3751263 returns 404/403 and cannot be resolved. No source confirms the exact title 'The Right to Regulate and the Second Amendment' by Cornell in Texas Law Review vol. 100. A real Cornell article with a similar but distinct title ('The Right to Regulate Arms in the Era of the Fourteenth Amendment') exists in UC Davis Law Review, suggesting the citation conflates or fabricates a combination of title and venue that does not correspond to any verifiable real publication.

The paper exists and all metadata (4 authors in correct order, year 2006, Epidemiology vol 17(3) pp 268-275, DOI) matches exactly. The title in the citation is wrong - the real title is 'Evaluating Short-Term Drug Effects Using a Physician-Specific Prescribing Preference as an Instrumental Variable', not 'physician-controlled randomized present-on-admission design' - but the remaining attribution unambiguously identifies the real work.

Three web searches returned no direct confirmation of this paper. JASN Volume 19(1) corresponds to 2008, not 2016 as cited, and the DOI encodes '2007' as the submission year -- both inconsistent with the cited year. The paper may exist with year 2008, but I cannot confirm or deny its existence within my search budget.

Tanzin v. Tanvir is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court case decided unanimously on December 10, 2020. Multiple authoritative sources including Wikipedia and Justia confirm the citation as 592 U.S. 43 (2020), matching the cited attribution exactly.

The STOP-IT trial (Study to Optimize Peritoneal Infection Therapy) is a real, well-known clinical trial by Sawyer et al. published in NEJM in 2015, not JAMA Surgery in 2018. Both acronym expansions given are incorrect, and the venue and year are wrong, but the trial name for intra-abdominal infection uniquely identifies the real work.

A Cochrane review on this topic exists (CD002958, 'Early postnatal discharge from hospital for healthy mothers and term infants'), but no version of it carries the cited title and no author named 'Coad' is associated with any version. The author name is not a garbled form of any actual author (Jones, Stewart, Taylor, Brown, Davis), so the citation as a whole does not identify any real work.

A Cochrane systematic review on cardioselective beta-blockers for COPD exists: Salpeter SR et al., 'Cardioselective beta-blockers for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease,' Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2005, CD003566.pub2 (DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD003566.pub2). The citation is a generic descriptive reference to this real review.

The book 'Government by Contract: Outsourcing and American Democracy' edited by Jody Freeman and Martha Minow was published by Harvard University Press in 2009 — confirmed by multiple authoritative sources including Harvard University Press, Harvard Law School, Cambridge Core, and Amazon.

Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971) is confirmed by Justia, Cornell LII, Oyez, and the Library of Congress. The reporter citation and year are exact. The cited title is a common shortened variant that drops 'Named' and rephrases the agency, but does not point to a different work.

Egbert v. Boule is a confirmed 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision at 596 U.S. 482 (2022), decided June 8, 2022. The '___' placeholder is the pre-pagination form of the same citation; the full paginated cite is 596 U.S. 482. Multiple authoritative sources (Supreme Court official site, Justia, Oyez) confirm the case name, year, and reporter volume.

No paper with the title 'Minimizing bias in antiarrhythmic drug trials' exists. A real Psaty & Siscovick JAMA 2010 paper does exist (PMID 20736474) but its actual title is 'Minimizing bias due to confounding by indication in comparative effectiveness research: the importance of restriction,' appearing in vol. 304(8) pp. 897-898. The cited title is not a minor garbling -- it invents a completely different subject matter (antiarrhythmic drugs) and the volume/issue/pages are all wrong.

Three targeted searches found no record of 'Kowalski v. Steelcase Inc.' in any legal database (CourtListener, Justia, Leagle, or otherwise). Volume 793 F.Supp.3d is indexed on Leagle confirming coverage of that range, yet no Kowalski v. Steelcase case appears at volume 817 or anywhere else. A published F.Supp.3d opinion would be publicly accessible.

Catherine M. Sharkey is a real NYU law professor, but her complete NYU faculty publications list contains no work titled 'The Agency Settle-or-Sue Decision' from 2011 or any other year. Two targeted web searches also returned no evidence of this article's existence anywhere on the open web.

The DOI 10.2139/ssrn.4096567 returns HTTP 404, no author named Matthew R. Schwinn appears in any legal scholarship search, and three independent searches found zero corroboration for this article in the Administrative Law Review or any other venue.

No evidence of this article exists across multiple targeted searches combining the authors (Bilz/Oseid), title, and venue (Yale Journal of Law & Technology Vol. 25, 2023). Kenworthey Bilz is a real scholar but her work focuses on law and psychology, not Bivens doctrine, and no co-authorship with an 'Eric Oseid' appears anywhere. The journal volume exists but this article does not appear in it.

Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296 (2018) is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court decision decided June 22, 2018, holding that obtaining historical cell-site location information without a warrant violates the Fourth Amendment. The reporter citation and year match official Supreme Court records.

The EPIC-HR trial (oral nirmatrelvir for high-risk COVID-19) is a real 2022 study (PMID 35172054), but it was published in the New England Journal of Medicine (doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2118542), not The Lancet Infectious Diseases. The venue attribution is demonstrably incorrect, so the citation as stated does not exist.
Collins v. Virginia, 584 U.S. 586 (2018) is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court decision, verified via Justia, Wikipedia, and Oyez. The volume, page number, and year all match the actual case.

The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test Manual by R. K. Heaton (1981) is a well-documented, widely-cited neuropsychological test manual published by Psychological Assessment Resources (Odessa, FL). Title, first-author surname, and year match exactly.

PubMed returns zero results for lead author Bouvette combined with bronchiectasis or Ontario. The article ID 8502127 cannot be confirmed at the Canadian Respiratory Journal publisher URL. While co-author T.K. Marras is a real respirologist at Toronto who works on lung disease in Ontario, no indexed record of this specific paper exists after three search attempts.

Collins v. Virginia is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court case decided in 2018 (584 U.S. 586, 138 S. Ct. 1663), concerning the Fourth Amendment automobile exception and warrantless searches of vehicles parked on curtilage. It is documented on Justia, Cornell LII, SCOTUSblog, and Oyez.

The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test Manual by Heaton (along with co-authors Chelune, Talley, Kay, and Curtiss) published in 1993 as a 'Revised and Expanded' edition is confirmed by multiple sources including Semantic Scholar, Open Library, and BibSonomy. The author, year, and title all match the cited work.

The article exists and is confirmed at the Michigan Law Review repository. The title, author (Orin S. Kerr), venue, volume (102), and issue (5) all match; however, the cited year (2018) is wrong -- the actual publication year is 2004 -- and the end page (853) is wrong -- the actual range is 801-888. These are metadata errors that do not change which work is being cited.

No evidence of Tsosie v. Peabody Western Coal Company exists in any federal case database, court records, or legal indexes. The reporter citation 836 F.4th 1129 appears associated with an unrelated immigration case, and known Peabody Western Coal litigation ran through the 9th Circuit and D. Arizona, not the 10th Circuit.

15 U.S.C. § 1692 exists as the congressional findings and declaration of purpose section of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA), confirmed via law.cornell.edu. The citation is correctly formed and unambiguously identifies a real statute.

Apple Inc. v. Pepper is a confirmed 2019 U.S. Supreme Court antitrust case. Multiple authoritative sources (Justia, SCOTUSblog, Wikipedia, supremecourt.gov) confirm the case exists, was decided May 13, 2019, and the citation 587 U.S. 273 (2019) is the correct U.S. Reports citation.

PubMed search for all three author surnames (Fowler, French, Screaton) combined with 'bronchiectasis' returned only a 2006 European Respiratory Journal paper (PMID 16807259), not any 2017 BMJ review article. No web evidence exists for a BMJ article with these authors, this title, and this year; the citation appears to borrow real author names from a different, real paper and assign them a fabricated 2017 BMJ title.

The article does not appear in the verified table of contents for Harvard Journal of Law & Technology Vol. 33(1) (Fall 2019), which lists eight pieces by other authors with no Skinner entry. The DOI prefix 10.1145 belongs exclusively to ACM, not Harvard, and the DOI itself returns 404. No independent source (Google Scholar, HeinOnline, or law review aggregator) surfaces this author-title combination.

The case name appears only as a broken Studicata link (404) with no corresponding entry in Justia, FindLaw, or any court docket. No primary legal source confirms or definitively refutes the existence of a civil case captioned Sivertson v. Citibank.

City of Canton v. Harris, 489 U.S. 378 (1989) is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court case decided February 28, 1989. The case name, reporter volume/page, and year all match exactly. The full official name is 'City of Canton, Ohio v. Harris' but the shortened form used in the citation is standard.

No trace of this specific article exists across three targeted searches, Carrier's own faculty bibliography, or any academic index. The citation combines verifiable real-world elements (author, case, journal, year) but the article itself cannot be located anywhere, matching the pattern of a hallucinated citation.

No trial named 'PEGASUS-PCI' exists in The Lancet or elsewhere. The real PEGASUS-TIMI 54 trial was published in NEJM in 2015; a PCI sub-analysis of that trial appeared in JAHA in 2020, not The Lancet. The cited title and venue combination does not correspond to any identifiable real publication.

No article by Hovenkamp titled 'The Open Economy: Understanding the New Antitrust Litigation' exists in the Yale Law Journal or any other source. Hovenkamp is a real antitrust scholar with confirmed YLJ publications, but none match this title, volume, or page range. Multiple searches across his bibliography, Penn Law faculty page, SSRN, and Yale Law Journal returned no trace of this work.

The case True Health Diagnostics, LLC v. Azar, 392 F. Supp. 3d 656 (E.D. Tex. 2019) is confirmed by vLex, CourtListener (docket 9:19-cv-00110), and Studicata. The reporter citation, court, and year all match.

No case at 861 F.3d 1366 (11th Cir. 2017) was found. The only confirmed ALPA/Delta 11th Circuit case at volume 861 is Delta Air Lines, Inc. v. Air Line Pilots Association, International, 861 F.2d 665 (11th Cir. 1989) -- a different reporter series (F.2d not F.3d), year (1989 not 2017), page number (665 not 1366), and reversed party order. The cited reporter string does not correspond to any real case.

Rubin's 1976 paper 'Inference and Missing Data' published in Biometrika 63:581-592 is a well-established, heavily cited work that introduced the taxonomy of missing data mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR). The citation's author, year, and topic match exactly.

The case Sivertson v. Citibank, N.A., 390 F. Supp. 3d 769 (E.D. Tex. 2019) exists and all cited metadata is confirmed: volume, page number, reporter, court, and year are accurate. 'Citibank, N.A.' is a conventional truncation of the full defendant name (which includes trustee capacity for a WaMu mortgage trust) and does not change which work is being cited.

Daniel A. Newman (2003) published 'Longitudinal Modeling with Randomly and Systematically Missing Data: A Simulation of Ad Hoc, Maximum Likelihood, and Multiple Imputation Techniques' in Organizational Research Methods (Vol. 6, No. 3, pp. 328-362), which is a precise match on author surname, year, and the described topic of missing data handling in longitudinal studies.

No case titled 'Communications Workers of America v. FCC' from 2021 can be found in any legal database. The closest real cases are two 2021 D.C. Circuit decisions styled 'Communications Workers of America v. National Labor Relations Board,' suggesting the cited case either misnames the opposing party or is a fabrication.

Both authors are real environmental law scholars who collaborate, and the venue/pagination are internally plausible, but no open-web source, faculty bibliography, or law review index confirms an article by this exact title in the Environmental Law Reporter in 2018. The only confirmed 2018 Ruhl-Salzman co-authored article is 'Presidential Exit' in the Duke Law Journal. The article may exist behind a closed paywall database, but cannot be verified or falsified without Westlaw/LexisNexis access.

A real Lancet systematic review by Coombes, Bisset, and Vicenzino exists, but it was published in 2010 (not 2015), vol. 376 pp. 1751-1767, DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61160-9. The cited year is off by 5 years, volume/issue/pages are all wrong, and the claimed DOI returns a 404. No 2015 Lancet paper by these authors on this topic was found.

Three targeted searches found no web-accessible record of this specific paper by Rodríguez-Merchán in a journal called 'Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology' (2016, 25(3), 231-242). The author is a real orthopedic surgeon but the exact title, journal, and volume metadata could not be confirmed or refuted within the search budget.

Craig K. Enders published 'Applied Missing Data Analysis' (Guilford Press, 2010), confirmed by ERIC, Google Books, and multiple bookseller records. The characterization 'with psychological examples' is accurate: Enders is a quantitative psychologist and the book targets psychology researchers with behavioral science datasets throughout.

The case E. Bay Sanctuary Covenant v. Barr, 391 F. Supp. 3d 974 (N.D. Cal. 2019) is confirmed by multiple legal databases including vLex, Justia, CourtListener, and the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse. All citation elements match: reporter citation (391 F. Supp. 3d 974), court (N.D. Cal.), and year (2019). The 'E. Bay' abbreviation for 'East Bay' is standard reporter style.

Kyle-Labell v. Selective Service System, 364 F. Supp. 3d 394 (D.N.J. 2019) is a confirmed real case (docket 2:15-cv-05193) in which plaintiff Elizabeth Kyle-Labell challenged the male-only Selective Service registration requirement on equal-protection grounds. The case name, court, and year all match the cited metadata exactly.

Ebbe v. Concorde Investment Services, LLC exists as a real 2019 federal case (392 F.Supp.3d 228), confirmed via vLex and Justia. The venue is D. Mass. (District of Massachusetts), not D.D.C. as cited, but this is a minor metadata error that does not prevent identification of the actual case.

The 2015 ESC Guidelines on pericardial diseases are confirmed as real, published in the European Heart Journal (vol. 36, issue 42, pp. 2921-64, November 2015) by the ESC Task Force. The cited title 'ESC Guidelines on pericarditis' is a minor simplification of the full title but the year and venue uniquely identify the work.

The case Weyerhaeuser Co. v. United States Fish and Wildlife Service exists and was decided in 2018 at 586 U.S. ___ (also cited as 139 S. Ct. 361). The case name and year are correct; the page number '9' may be unconfirmed pending final bound-volume pagination, but this is a minor metadata discrepancy that does not change which case is being cited.

Kamenov is a real PCOS/inositol researcher, but three targeted searches found no 2018 Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism paper by Kamenov on inositol plus metformin for ovulation improvement. His documented work involves inositol plus clomiphene citrate or inositol versus metformin, not the combined inositol-plus-metformin formulation described, and appears in other journals. Insufficient positive evidence to confirm or definitively refute.

Environmental Law vol. 49, issue 1 (2019) contains no article by Nagle with this title; the actual table of contents lists seven articles by entirely different authors. The DOI resolves to a 404, and the real scholar whose name closely matches (John Copeland Nagle) passed away in May 2019 with no 2019 publications on record.

Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education, 526 U.S. 629 (1999) is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court decision. The reporter citation, case name, and year all match authoritative sources including Justia and the Library of Congress. Justice O'Connor wrote for a 5-4 majority on Title IX student-on-student harassment liability.

Gebser v. Lago Vista Independent School District, 524 U.S. 274 (1998) is a real U.S. Supreme Court decision decided June 22, 1998, holding 5-4 on Title IX teacher-student harassment liability. The case name, reporter citation, and year all match exactly across Justia, Cornell LII, and FindLaw.

Auer v. Robbins is a real Supreme Court case but its correct citation is 519 U.S. 452 (1997), not 514 U.S. 938 (1995). The cited reporter citation (514 U.S. 938) resolves to a completely different case, First Options of Chicago, Inc. v. Kaplan (1995), matching the EXISTENT_WRONG_ID failure mode.

GenBand US LLC v. Metaswitch Networks Ltd., 248 F. Supp. 3d 825 (E.D. Tex. 2017) is confirmed by CourtListener and Leagle.com. The case name, reporter volume and page, court (Eastern District of Texas, docket 2:16-CV-00582-JRG before Judge Gilstrap), and year (decided March 31, 2017) all match exactly.

No Cochrane review on cannabis-based medicines was published or updated in 2014. The real 2014 systematic review on cannabis and neurologic conditions is by Koppel et al. in Neurology (an AAN product, not Cochrane). The Cochrane anti-spasticity review (Shakespeare et al., CD001332) dates to 2003, and the Cochrane cannabis/MS review (Filippini et al., CD013444) was published in 2022, neither matching the claimed 2014 Cochrane cannabis-based medicines update.

No case named 'Mensah v. Delta Air Lines, Inc.' exists in any legal database for N.D. Ga. 2020. The reporter citation '838 F. Supp. 3d' is technically impossible for a 2020 decision (F. Supp. 3d had only reached volumes ~400-500 by that year), and page 8124 exceeds any plausible reporter page number. The closest real citation found is O'Hern v. Delta Airlines, 838 F. Supp. 1264 (N.D. Ill. 1993), a different case from a different series entirely.

Multiple authoritative legal databases (Justia, FindLaw, CourtListener, PACER) confirm Brothers and Sisters in Christ, LLC v. Zazzle, Inc. is a real 8th Circuit 2022 decision (No. 21-1917, decided August 2, 2022) involving trademark infringement and personal jurisdiction. The case name, venue, and year all match the citation exactly.

American Airlines, Inc. v. Wolens, 513 U.S. 219 (1995) is a real U.S. Supreme Court case decided January 18, 1995. The case name, volume, reporter, page, and year all match exactly. It concerned whether the Airline Deregulation Act preempted state-law claims arising from changes to a frequent flyer program.

The Journal of Free Speech Law is a real journal founded by Eugene Volokh, but no article matching this title exists in it. The journal's volume numbering began at Volume 1 in 2021, making a '12(3)' citation for a 2022 article structurally impossible. No trace of the cited title or any 'Zazzle decision' article by Volokh was found.

42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5 is a real, extant section of the U.S. Code (Title VII enforcement provisions) confirmed at law.cornell.edu and uscode.house.gov; subsection (e) specifically addresses EEOC charge-filing time limits and is a widely cited statutory provision.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 is a well-documented US federal law, confirmed by official government sources including the EEOC (eeoc.gov), Department of Labor (dol.gov), and National Archives. It is a real component of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, covering employment discrimination protections.

No case matching 'Sobieski v. Hyatt Hotels Corporation' appears in any legal database (Justia, CourtListener, or open web searches). Additionally, the reporter citation is impossible: F. Supp. 3d volume 833 does not exist, as the series had only reached the mid-to-high 700s as of mid-2026, and page 2569 within a single volume is implausibly high.

The Harvard Journal of Law & Technology Vol. 35, No. 2 (Spring 2022) table of contents contains four articles with no mention of Citron, Chesney, or this title. Citron and Chesney's documented collaborations are limited to deepfakes topics (2018-2020), not Section 230, and no article matching this title appears anywhere on the open web.

Multiple sources confirm the case exists as cited: Justia dockets it as case 21-4039 in the Tenth Circuit, Casemine lists it as 'Chilcoat v. San Juan Cnty. | No. 21-4039 | 10th Cir.', and the search results explicitly reference the citation '41 F.4th 1196, 1214 (10th Cir. 2022)' matching the cited reporter volume, page, court, and year exactly.

No paper titled 'Influenza Vaccination and Mortality in Acute Heart Failure study' exists in JAMA Cardiology (2019) or any other venue. The closest real paper is Rodrigues et al., 'Influenza Vaccination and Outcome in Heart Failure,' published in the American Journal of Cardiology in 2020 -- a different title, venue, and year. The differences are too substantial to constitute mere metadata errors.
Obergefell v. Hodges is a confirmed US Supreme Court decision from 2015, reported at 576 U.S. 644 (2015). The case name and year match exactly.

Fort Bend County v. Davis, 587 U.S. 541 (2019) is confirmed as a real U.S. Supreme Court decision decided June 3, 2019, with the exact reporter citation (volume 587, page 541) matching the Supreme Court's own official preliminary print documents. The case is a unanimous Title VII decision authored by Justice Ginsburg.

The case Tech Pharmacy Servs., LLC v. Alixa RX LLC exists exactly as cited: 298 F. Supp. 3d 892, Eastern District of Texas, decided December 22, 2017 (docket 4:15-CV-00766). All citation elements -- case name, reporter volume and page, court, and year -- are confirmed by vLex, CourtListener, and Justia.

The Natural Gas Act (NGA) is a well-established US federal statute enacted June 21, 1938 (52 Stat. 821), codified at 15 U.S.C. Chapter 15B (§ 717 et seq.), and administered by FERC. It is authoritatively documented on law.cornell.edu, govinfo.gov, and ferc.gov.

No public record of 'Petrov v. ExxonMobil Pipeline Company' was found in the Northern District of Texas across three targeted searches covering Justia, PacerMonitor, and general web sources. Absence of web evidence is not positive proof of fabrication, as the case could be unreported or require PACER access; however, there is no corroborating evidence to confirm existence.

Section 1(b) of the Natural Gas Act is a real statutory provision codified at 15 U.S.C. § 717(b), confirmed by the LII/Cornell legal database and the U.S. House Office of Law Revision Counsel. It defines federal jurisdictional scope over natural gas transportation and sales in interstate commerce.

Saba Mahmood's 'Politics of Piety: The Islamic Revival and the Feminist Subject' was published by Princeton University Press in 2005, confirmed by multiple authoritative sources including the Princeton University Press catalog. Author surname, title, and year all match the citation exactly.

Three searches returned no match for a Horning-authored work titled 'Study of Spontaneous Tumours in Rat Strains' from the 1970s. A 'Burrows and Horning, 1952' appears in an adjacent area, but the specific 1970s title cannot be confirmed or ruled out given the vague attribution (no journal, no year, no DOI).
The case Hall Arts Ctr. Office, LLC v. Hanover Ins. Co. at 327 F. Supp. 3d 979 (N.D. Tex. 2018) was found on CaseMine with the exact case name and reporter citation matching the cited attribution.
CourtListener lists 'Gary Miller v. New York & New Jersey Port Aut' at 351 F. Supp. 3d 762, D.N.J., which matches the cited case name, reporter citation, court, and year exactly.

Numerical Recipes in C is a well-documented real book published by Cambridge University Press, authored by W.H. Press, S.A. Teukolsky, W.T. Vetterling, and B.P. Flannery. All four cited author surnames match the real authors exactly.

Three targeted searches found no indexed source confirming a 1970 paper by Horning et al. with this title. The paper may be a pre-digital journal article not indexed online, but no positive evidence of existence or non-existence was found.

No web-accessible source confirms the existence of this article, the title, or the author 'H. J. Polisky' in connection with the Texas Bar Journal or any Texas legal publication. The metadata is internally plausible (Vol. 82 does correspond to 2019), but the complete absence of any trace in public indexes, legal databases, or attorney directories means the citation can be neither confirmed nor refuted without access to Westlaw/LexisNexis or the physical journal.

Liang et al.'s adaptive optics wavefront sensing work on the human eye is a well-documented landmark series: Liang et al. 1994 (first wavefront sensing in the eye) and Liang, Williams, Miller 1997 ('Supernormal vision and high-resolution retinal imaging through adaptive optics,' JOSA). The cited year of 1990 is a metadata error, but the contextual description 'late 1990s' correctly identifies the timeframe, and the author + topic uniquely identify this real work.

Impression Products, Inc. v. Lexmark International, Inc., 137 S. Ct. 1523 (2017) is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court decision decided May 30, 2017, on patent exhaustion. The reporter citation 137 S. Ct. 1523 and year 2017 are correct per Justia, WIPO Lex, Quimbee, and the official Supreme Court opinion. The only variation is 'Co.' vs 'Inc.' in the petitioner name, which is a minor transcription variant that does not affect identification of the case.

Both Thibos and Porter are real, established researchers who have published multiple peer-reviewed articles and review-type works on wavefront aberrations in human eyes, confirmed via searches of PubMed and JOSA. The citation is a general attribution to known authors in the field rather than a specific fabricated title.

The Yale Journal of Law & Technology Volume 20 table of contents lists seven articles, none of which is by an author named Wang and none concerns patent exhaustion or the repair-reconstruction distinction. Three searches and a direct fetch of the journal's Volume 20 page produced no trace of this article anywhere on the open web, and the volume's actual contents directly contradict the citation's claimed venue, volume, and page range.

No evidence of this article exists online. The DOI prefix 10.1017 belongs to Cambridge University Press, but the Journal of Insurance Regulation is published by the NAIC and would never carry a Cambridge DOI. The DOI resolves to a 404, the volume/issue format (39(2)) does not match how JIR structures its publications, and no web search returned any trace of this article by Crawford & Summers.

The article 'Copying in Patent Law' by Cotropia and Lemley does exist in the North Carolina Law Review, Vol. 87, and is confirmed at scholarship.law.unc.edu. However, the year (2009, not 2013), issue (5, not 4), and page numbers (1421+, not 841-916) are all incorrect metadata. The title, authors, and venue still uniquely identify the real work.

Exhaustive PubMed and web searches found no record of this paper, but the JNM URL for volume 44(8) page 1291 returned HTTP 403 (access-controlled rather than absent), making definitive non-existence impossible to confirm. The author pair Naganawa + Kimura is real and collaborates on brain PET work, but no 2003 JNM paper matching this title was located.

The paper 'State-of-the-art review on laser cladding process as an in-situ repair technique' by Dhiraj Raj et al. was published online in 2021 (with formal journal publication in 2022 in Proc. IMechE Part E). The cited title is a shortened form of the real title, and 'Raj' matches the first author exactly. Year 2021 corresponds to the online-first publication date encoded in the DOI.

Sessions v. Dimaya, 584 U.S. 148 (2018) is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court decision handed down on April 17, 2018, holding 18 U.S.C. 16(b) unconstitutionally vague. The reporter citation, case name, and year all match across multiple authoritative sources including Justia, FindLaw, and Cornell LII.

No record of this paper exists at the cited coordinates. The Journal of Nuclear Cardiology was founded in 1994, making Volume 7 correspond to approximately year 2000, not 2006, so the volume-year pairing is internally inconsistent. Three web searches and PubMed checks found no matching paper by this author group in this journal at any year.

A paper by Dhiraj Raj et al. titled 'State-of-the-art review on laser cladding process as an in-situ repair technique' (Sage/IMECHE, DOI 10.1177/09544089211044558) exists and was published online in 2021. Chilcoat v. San Juan County, 41 F.4th 1196 (10th Cir. 2022) is confirmed by CourtListener's official F.4th volume index, the 10th Circuit docket (case no. 21-4039), Justia, and an official court opinion PDF. The case name, reporter, court, and year all match exactly.

Three targeted web searches produced no results matching this article by Kassel in the Georgetown Law Journal or any other venue. No positive evidence of existence or non-existence was found; the article may exist in databases not indexed by general web search.

Three targeted searches found no trial specifically named 'SMART-C' published in 2020. The primary SMART-C entity found is the SGLT2i Meta-Analysis Cardio-Renal Trialists' Consortium, established in 2022 and published in Circulation in 2024, not 2020. No positive evidence of fabrication was found, but no 2020 SMART-C publication could be confirmed.

No publication matching Muntner + NHANES III + American Journal of Kidney Diseases + 2003 exists in PubMed (zero results on direct query). The closest real Muntner paper on renal insufficiency and cardiovascular mortality uses NHANES II data, was published in JASN in 2002, not AJKD in 2003. The citation appears to be a composite of real elements assembled incorrectly.

No trial named 'PEGASUS-PCI' exists on the open web. The real trial is 'PEGASUS-TIMI 54,' a ticagrelor vs. placebo RCT in prior-MI patients. The cited name conflates the PEGASUS acronym with 'PCI' (percutaneous coronary intervention), which does not match any known trial name or substudy designation.

CourtListener and Justia both confirm this case exists at exactly 359 F. Supp. 3d 423, decided by the Eastern District of Virginia on February 12, 2019, with the docket number 1:18-cv-677. All cited metadata matches.

5 U.S.C. § 553 is the Administrative Procedure Act's rulemaking section and definitively exists. The cited subsection (b)(3)(B) refers to the well-known 'good cause' exception to notice-and-comment rulemaking, which is a real provision. While the technically precise citation may be 5 U.S.C. § 553(b)(B), the form '(b)(3)(B)' is widely used in court opinions and legal practice to unambiguously identify this same provision.

A real Sarnak-affiliated paper exists in Kidney International in 2003 ('Level of kidney function as a risk factor for cardiovascular outcomes in the elderly,' PMID 12631096), but it uses the Cardiovascular Health Study cohort, not the Framingham Heart Study as the citation claims. No Sarnak et al. 2003 Kidney International paper analyzing Framingham Heart Study data on CKD and cardiovascular mortality could be found; the Framingham descriptor does not match any real paper at those bibliographic coordinates.

Weyerhaeuser Co. v. United States Fish and Wildlife Service is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court case decided November 27, 2018, with the citation 586 U.S. 9 verified by the Supreme Court's own preliminary print of Volume 586, Part 1. The parallel citation is 139 S. Ct. 361 (2018). All metadata matches.

Kennedy v. Bremerton School District is a confirmed 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision (decided June 27, 2022), reported at 597 U.S. 507. The citation's use of '___' instead of '507' is the standard placeholder format for newly decided cases and does not affect identification.

A contemporaneous book-received notice confirms G. A. F. Seber published 'The Estimation of Animal Abundance and Related Parameters' in 1982 with Charles Griffin & Co. Ltd (abbreviated as 'Charles Griffin' in the citation). This is the second edition; the first appeared in 1973 from the same publisher.

The paper exists and all cited metadata is confirmed: Otis, D.L. et al. (1978), 'Statistical inference from capture data on closed animal populations,' Wildlife Monographs 62, pp. 1-135. Verified via JSTOR (stable/3830650) and USGS publication records.

Eisgruber and Sager's 'Religious Freedom and the Constitution' is a real book published by Harvard University Press (first edition ~2007), not a Harvard Law Review article. No evidence of a 2022 Harvard Law Review article (vol. 135, issue 5) by these authors with this title was found in any search.

Glen H. Elder Jr.'s 'Children of the Great Depression' was published in 1974 by the University of Chicago Press, confirmed by multiple sources including Archive.org, Amazon, and publisher listings. The title, author surname (Elder), and year (1974) all match exactly.

The book 'Yoghurt: Science and Technology' (2nd ed., 1999) by A. Y. Tamime and R. K. Robinson, published by Woodhead Publishing, is confirmed real across multiple independent sources including Amazon (ISBN 1855733992), Wiley Online Library, and Google Books. All metadata matches exactly.

No evidence found that this article exists anywhere on the open web. Searches of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law (volume 58, 2020), David A. Martin's documented publication record, and direct title searches all return zero matches. Martin's confirmed 2020 work is an unrelated piece ('Taming Immigration'), and volume 58 of the journal surfaces unrelated articles.

The Evolut Low Risk Trial is a real, large randomized controlled trial (NCT02701283) evaluating Medtronic's Evolut TAVR system vs. surgery in low-risk aortic stenosis patients. It is widely cited in peer-reviewed literature including JACC and PubMed/PMC, with published outcomes at 2, 5, and 6 years.

Three targeted searches returned no results matching 'Bowers v. Kijakazi' at 40 F.4th 872 (8th Cir. 2022). Similar Kijakazi appeals in the 8th Circuit and surrounding volumes were found, but this specific case name and citation did not surface on Justia, CourtListener, or general web searches. Absence from these databases is suspicious for a published circuit opinion, but no positive evidence of fabrication was found.

The article 'Religious Liberty and the Culture Wars' by Douglas Laycock exists but was published in the 2014 University of Illinois Law Review at page 839, not in the Notre Dame Law Review in 2022. The cited DOI (10.34996/ndlr.98.2.681) returns HTTP 404, and Notre Dame Law Review Vol. 98, Issue 2 contains no such article. The citation grafts a real author/title onto a fabricated journal, year, volume, and page range.

Carpenter v. United States (585 U.S. 296, 2018) is a confirmed, well-documented U.S. Supreme Court case widely described as a landmark Fourth Amendment ruling on cell phone location data privacy. Multiple authoritative legal sources confirm its existence and landmark status.

Carpenter v. United States is a confirmed, landmark U.S. Supreme Court case decided June 22, 2018 (585 U.S. 296), holding that government access to historical cell site location information requires a warrant under the Fourth Amendment. It is verifiable via the Supreme Court's official opinion and multiple authoritative legal databases.

The book 'Immigration and Refugee Law and Policy' (6th ed.) by Legomsky and Rodriguez, published by Foundation Press, is a real and well-established casebook. However, the 6th edition was published in 2015, not 2021; by 2021 the current edition was the 7th (2019), co-authored with a different second author. The year is a metadata error, but the title, both author surnames, edition number, and publisher still uniquely identify the cited work.

The book 'Forensic Science: An Introduction to Scientific and Investigative Techniques' 3rd ed. (2009, CRC Press, ISBN 9781420064933) clearly exists with editors James and Nordby. 'Madea' does not appear as an editor of this edition, but the title, year, venue, and first two editors correctly identify the real work, making this a metadata error rather than a fabricated citation.

Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296 (2018) is confirmed by Wikipedia, Justia, and the official Supreme Court PDF. The case name, page citation, and year are all accurate. It is a 5-4 decision by Chief Justice Roberts decided June 22, 2018.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b) is a well-established, real rule in the U.S. Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, confirmed by authoritative sources including Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute and the U.S. Courts website. It requires particularity in pleading fraud or mistake claims.

The book exists as confirmed by multiple sources (AbeBooks, Biblio, Internet Archive, Routledge/CRC Press). The full title is 'Lee and Gaensslen's Advances in Fingerprint Technology' (3rd ed., 2012, CRC Press, edited by Robert S. Ramotowski). The citation omits the 'Lee and Gaensslen's' prefix but otherwise correctly identifies the work with matching editor surname, year, edition, and publisher.

The EPIC-HR trial (Evaluation of Protease Inhibition for COVID-19 in High-Risk Patients) is a well-documented Phase 2/3 Pfizer clinical trial for Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir), confirmed by multiple sources including Pfizer press releases and peer-reviewed literature. The acronym expansion matches exactly.

Two distinct real Cochrane reviews exist: 'Interventions for preventing obesity in children' by Summerbell et al. (CD001871, 2005) and 'Interventions for treating obesity in children' by Oude Luttikhuis et al. (CD001872, 2009). The citation combines the title of the first with the author of the second, meaning the byline names a different real paper than the one the title identifies.

A real 1949 Biochemical Journal series on potato eelworm hatching factor exists with 'D H Marrian' as a co-author, but 'George Frederick Marrian' does not match any confirmed author in that series. George/Guy Frederic Marrian (G.F. Marrian) was a steroid biochemist with no known connection to eelworm research. The exact cited title does not appear verbatim in any confirmed paper from the series.

Lesnik v. Eisenmann SE, 374 F. Supp. 3d 923 (N.D. Cal. 2019) is confirmed to exist. The case was decided March 20, 2019 by Judge Lucy H. Koh in the Northern District of California (Case No. 16-CV-01120-LHK), and the exact reporter citation matches across vLex, CourtListener, and Leagle.

Volume 835 of the F.3d reporter dates to 2016, making it impossible for a 2021 D.C. Circuit decision to appear there. No case named 'American Hospital Association v. CMS' exists at 835 F.3d 1018; real AHA cases against CMS-related defendants use different captions (v. Azar, v. Becerra) and appear in F.4th for 2021 decisions.

The case Make The Road New York v. Chad F. Wolf, 962 F.3d 612 (D.C. Cir. 2020) is confirmed by multiple authoritative legal databases including Justia, CourtListener, Leagle, and the Senate Judiciary Committee website. The reporter citation, court, and year all match exactly.

International Shoe Co. v. Washington is a landmark US Supreme Court decision at 326 U.S. 310 (1945), consistently confirmed across authoritative legal sources including Justia, LII, and FindLaw. The case is well-known for establishing the 'minimum contacts' standard for personal jurisdiction.

The cited 'STOP trial (Short Treatment of Intra-abdominal Infection)' clearly refers to the real STOP-IT trial ('Trial of Short-Course Antimicrobial Therapy for Intraabdominal Infection,' Sawyer RG et al., NEJM 2015;372:1996-2005). The 2018 date corresponds to a published correction notice, the acronym is truncated (STOP vs STOP-IT), and the title is paraphrased but points unambiguously to the same work. These are metadata errors that do not change which work is being cited.

The case Joshua Atchley v. AstraZeneca UK Limited, 22 F.4th 204 (D.C. Cir. 2022) is confirmed by Justia, FindLaw, vLex, and other sources. The case name, reporter citation, court, and year all match exactly. It is a D.C. Circuit decision from January 4, 2022, docket no. 20-7077, concerning Anti-Terrorism Act / JASTA liability.

The EPIC-HR trial was published in NEJM as 'Oral Nirmatrelvir for High-Risk, Nonhospitalized Adults with Covid-19' (Hammond et al., NEJM 2022;386:1397-1408, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2118542). The venue is correct and the trial name uniquely identifies the work; the year is off by one (2021 vs actual 2022), which falls within the ±1 tolerance for metadata errors.

Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Court of California is a confirmed U.S. Supreme Court decision from June 19, 2017 (582 U.S. ___, docket 16-466), addressing specific personal jurisdiction under the Due Process Clause. It is documented across the Supreme Court's own website, Justia, Cornell LII, Oyez, and SCOTUSblog.

The textbook 'Evolution' by Carl T. Bergstrom and Lee Alan Dugatkin, published by W.W. Norton & Company, exists and is a well-known evolutionary biology textbook. The 1st edition was published in 2012 and a 2nd edition in 2015/2016, so the citation conflates the 1st edition year (2012) with the 2nd edition label -- a metadata error that does not change which work is being cited.

The title 'Chevron's Domain' belongs to a 2001 Georgetown Law Journal article by Thomas W. Merrill and Kristin E. Hickman, not Elena Kagan. No article by Kagan under this title in the Harvard Law Review Forum (volume 134 or otherwise) appears in any search result or the HLR author archive. The citation appears to be a fabrication that grafts a real article title onto a prominent author and plausible venue.

The book 'Molecular Genetics of Bacteria' by Snyder and Champness exists and was published in 2007, matching the cited title, first-author surname, and year. Two metadata errors are present: the cited edition is '4th' but 2007 is the 3rd edition, and the publisher is ASM Press (not Sinauer Associates). These errors do not change which work is being cited, as title+author+year uniquely identify the real work.

The DESTINY-Breast03 primary results paper by Cortés et al. was published in the New England Journal of Medicine (2022;386(12):1143-1154), not Lancet Oncology. No publication matching the cited journal, volume, issue, and pages exists; the citation appears to be a hallucination combining real trial and author details with a completely wrong venue and pagination.

The Fair Housing Act is a real and well-established US federal law (Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, 42 U.S.C. Chapter 45), confirmed by official government sources including the DOJ, HUD, and the US Code.

Both the FDA and the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) are real, well-established regulatory bodies that produce pharmaceutical guidelines. The FDA publishes and adopts ICH guidelines as official guidance for industry, confirmed by FDA.gov and multiple Federal Register entries. The citation is a broad reference to these organizations' guidelines, not a fabricated entity.

Three web searches across legal databases (Justia, Leagle, LII) and general web found no case pairing 'Antonescu' with 'Philadelphia Gas Works' in any court, any year. Real Philadelphia Gas Works cases exist but none involve a party named Antonescu. No docket number, reporter citation, or court is provided, and no corroborating source of any kind surfaced.

Kaplan's Clinical Hypertension is a well-documented, long-standing medical textbook by Norman M. Kaplan, with at least 11 editions published by Lippincott Williams & Wilkins/Wolters Kluwer. Multiple authoritative sources confirm its existence and authorship.

The DOI 10.2139/ssrn.3697156 returns HTTP 404, no SSRN record exists at that abstract_id, and Peter H. Schuck's official Yale Law School CV (read in full through August 2023) contains no article matching this title, venue, or year. The Yale Journal on Regulation website also shows no Schuck DACA article for 2020.

Multiple Cochrane reviews on sodium restriction demonstrably exist in the Cochrane Library, including at least one specific systematic review on altered dietary salt intake for diabetic kidney disease (Hodson, 2023). The citation is a general reference to a body of Cochrane work rather than a single paper, and that body of work is real and findable.

The citation lacks all identifying metadata (no authors, year, venue, or DOI). Multiple real published works exist at the intersection of community engagement ethics and relational autonomy in research ethics, but none can be identified as the single specific work being cited. The description is too generic to uniquely identify any one source.

Both Sandra Soo-Jin Lee and Adrienne Asch are confirmed real bioethics scholars, but the citation provides no specific title, year, venue, or DOI. No joint publication between these two scholars on community engagement and ethical considerations in clinical trials was found, and their primary documented research areas (genomics ethics and disability/reproductive ethics respectively) do not closely match the described topic.

Arthur C. Guyton was a real physiologist at the University of Mississippi Medical Center who published extensively on long-term blood pressure regulation models from the late 1950s through the 1970s. His landmark 1972 large-scale computer model of circulatory control is well-documented and remains foundational in hypertension research. The citation accurately describes his body of work.

Regulation DD (Truth in Savings) is a real and current US federal regulation codified at 12 C.F.R. Part 1030, confirmed by multiple authoritative sources including the CFPB, eCFR, and Cornell LII. The title, venue, and section number all match exactly.

The Truth in Savings Act is a real federal statute codified at 12 U.S.C. Chapter 44 (§§ 4301-4313). The cited section number §4701 is incorrect (should be §4301), but this is a digit transposition error that does not change which law is being cited -- the title 'Truth in Savings Act' and 'Title 12 U.S.C.' unambiguously identify the real statute.

The case Ecological Rights Foundation v. Federal Emergency Management Agency, 384 F. Supp. 3d 1111 (N.D. Cal. 2019) is confirmed by Leagle with an exact match on case name, reporter citation, court, and year. The case was decided May 15, 2019 by Judge James Donato on docket 3:16-cv-07252.

The LoDoCo trial exists as 'Low-Dose Colchicine for Secondary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease,' published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology in 2013 (Nidorf et al., JACC 61:404-410, DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2012.10.027). The cited title is a truncated but unambiguous reference to this well-known randomized controlled trial.

The Rechtschaffen & Kales 1968 manual is a well-established foundational reference in sleep medicine, confirmed by WorldCat (OCLC 14500597), Internet Archive, and Semantic Scholar. The title, authors, and year all match exactly. It was published by the Public Health Service, US Government Printing Office.

No evidence of 'Achebe v. KeyBank National Association' exists in any indexed legal database (Google Scholar, CourtListener, Leagle, Justia). The reporter citation '816 F. Supp. 3d 1682' also returns zero hits across all sources. Additionally, F. Supp. 3d volume 816 did not exist in 2020 (the series was in the ~400-500 volume range then), and page 1682 within a single volume is implausibly high.

A real paper with a similar title exists in Nature ('Tracking Tumor Evolution in Glioma through Liquid Biopsies of Cerebrospinal Fluid' by Miller et al., 2019), but the claimed first author 'Mateo' does not appear anywhere in the actual author list, and the year is off by 4 years (2015 vs. 2019). These are not minor metadata errors but fundamental attribution failures that prevent the citation from pointing to the real work.

The title 'NAMD2: Greater Scalability for Parallel Molecular Dynamics' belongs to a real 1999 paper by Kalé et al. in the Journal of Computational Physics; the attributed authors (Phillips, Braun, Wang, Tajkhorshid, Schulten), year (2005), and venue (Journal of Computational Chemistry) belong to a different real paper titled 'Scalable molecular dynamics with NAMD.' The citation merges the title of one real paper with the byline of a different real paper, constituting an EXISTENT_WRONG_ID fabrication.

The ASCENT trial exists as a real phase 3 RCT published in 2021, studying sacituzumab govitecan in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. The title and year uniquely identify the work, though the venue is incorrect: it was published in the New England Journal of Medicine (doi: 10.1056/NEJMoa2028485), not The Lancet Oncology. Per the taxonomy, this is a metadata error that does not change which work is being cited.

The case True Health Diagnostics, LLC v. Azar, 392 F. Supp. 3d 656 (E.D. Tex. 2019) is confirmed to exist with all citation details matching: case name, reporter volume (392), reporter (F. Supp. 3d), page (656), court (E.D. Tex., Lufkin Division), and year (2019, decided July 22). The case involved THD suing HHS Secretary Azar over suspension of Medicare payments.
The book exists exactly as cited. Full author is Saba Mahmood, published by Princeton University Press in 2005. Title, author surname, and year all match perfectly.

No authoritative source confirms a case styled 'Bowers v. Kijakazi' at 40 F.4th 872 (8th Cir. 2022). The cite.case.law redirect for that reporter citation returned a 404, and searches across CourtListener, Justia, and the Eighth Circuit's own site returned no matching case. While contextually plausible (F.4th began 2021, Kijakazi was SSA Commissioner in 2022), absence of any confirming result across multiple legal databases prevents verification within the 3-search budget.

The J-ALEX trial (alectinib vs crizotinib in ALK-positive NSCLC) is a real phase 3 RCT published in The Lancet in 2017. The citation has a venue error (Lancet Oncology vs The Lancet, both in the same journal family) and a year off by one (2018 vs 2017), but the trial name uniquely identifies the real work, making these mere metadata errors.

Three targeted searches found no trace of an article by Greacen with this title in the Food and Drug Law Journal. The journal itself is real and volume 75 (2020) is plausible, but the specific article and author cannot be confirmed or denied because legal journal content is largely paywalled and not fully indexed on the open web.

No paper titled 'Low-Dose Colchicine for Secondary Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease' was published in JACC in 2020. The actual LoDoCo2 trial was published in NEJM 2020 under the title 'Colchicine in Patients with Chronic Coronary Disease.' The cited title more closely resembles the original LoDoCo trial published in JACC in 2013, making this citation a conflation of two distinct papers that does not uniquely identify either real work.

Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386 (1989) is a real and well-known U.S. Supreme Court decision. Multiple authoritative sources (Justia, FindLaw, Cornell LII, Library of Congress, GovInfo) confirm the exact citation including case name, reporter, volume, page number, and year.

The case exists at 386 F. Supp. 3d 1132 (N.D. Cal. 2019), decided May 2019 by Judge Edward M. Chen. The only deviation is a shortened defendant name ('City of San Francisco' vs. the official 'City and County of San Francisco'), which is a common abbreviation that still uniquely identifies this case.

42 U.S.C. § 1983 is a well-established, real federal statute (Civil Rights Act of 1871) confirmed by authoritative sources including law.cornell.edu and uscode.house.gov. The citation accurately identifies Title 42, Section 1983 of the United States Code.

Three targeted searches found no evidence of a Bagley article titled 'Procedural Common Law' in the Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics. Bagley's verified 2019 publication is 'The Procedure Fetish' in the Michigan Law Review, but absence of web evidence for this specific title and venue does not constitute positive proof of non-existence.

McCoy v. Louisiana, 584 U.S. 414 (2018) is confirmed as a real U.S. Supreme Court case decided on May 14, 2018, holding that the Sixth Amendment guarantees a defendant the right to insist on maintaining innocence even against counsel's advice. The reporter citation (584 U.S. 414) and year (2018) match exactly across multiple authoritative sources including Justia, Cornell LII, and SCOTUSblog.

Monell v. Department of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978) is a verified U.S. Supreme Court decision decided June 6, 1978. The reporter citation and year are confirmed by Cornell LII, the Library of Congress, and Oyez.

The case Brown v. Serenity C&C, Inc., 391 F.Supp.3d 546 (E.D. Va. 2019) is confirmed to exist. Search results from vLex identify it as Civil No. 4:18cv112, decided July 17, 2019 in the Eastern District of Virginia, matching all cited metadata.

The Journal of Emergency Medical Services (JEMS) is a real, long-running professional publication with ISSN 0197-2510, published by Elsevier and confirmed via its official website jems.com and library catalog records.

The case Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. State Energy Resources Conservation & Development Commission, 461 U.S. 190 (1983), is a well-documented U.S. Supreme Court case confirmed by multiple authoritative legal sources including Justia, LII/Cornell, Oyez, and Wikipedia. The abbreviated citation 'PG&E v. State Energy Resources Conservation & Development Commission' is a standard shorthand for this real case.

Pazol v. Tough Mudder (2016) is a confirmed real case and the Journal of Legal Aspects of Sport is a real journal, but no web search returned any trace of the specific Bagdasarian article at 30(2), 145-167. The journal appears sparsely indexed online, so absence of results is not positive evidence of fabrication.

The Wendell H. Ford Aviation Investment and Reform Act for the 21st Century (AIR21) is a confirmed U.S. federal statute, and 49 U.S.C. § 42121 is the correct statutory section for its airline safety whistleblower protection provisions, as confirmed by multiple authoritative government sources including DOL, OSHA, and the FAA.

No web evidence of this specific article exists after 3 searches. The DOI prefix 10.1016 is exclusively registered to Elsevier, but Sports Lawyers Journal is published by the Sports Lawyers Association (not Elsevier), making it impossible for a legitimate article in that journal to carry this DOI. Matthew Mitten is a real sports law scholar, but this article does not appear in any publicly accessible record of his work.

The TIM-HF (Telemedical Interventional Monitoring in Heart Failure) trial is a real, well-documented RCT published by Koehler et al. in Circulation in 2011. The title and acronym are correct; the year 2017 is a metadata error (likely confusion with the TIM-HF2 follow-up trial published in The Lancet in 2018), but the citation unambiguously identifies the real study.

Pazol v. Tough Mudder Inc. is a real case (originating in D. Mass., 1st Cir. 2016), and a Studicata case brief suggests a second related proceeding exists, but I could not confirm the specific reporter citation 384 F. Supp. 3d 191 or the D.D.C. venue from open-web sources within the 3-search budget.

A real 2002 paper by Coad, Al-Rasasi, and Morgan exists ('Nutrient insult in early pregnancy,' Proceedings of the Nutrition Society), but the citation changes the title's key phrase from 'early pregnancy' to 'infancy' and misattributes it to the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. These are substantive errors that prevent the citation from identifying the real work.

The Telemedical Interventional Monitoring in Heart Failure (TIM-HF) study is a real trial, but the primary results were published in Circulation in 2011 (PMID 21444883), not in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2017. The successor trial TIM-HF2 was published in The Lancet in 2018. No version of this study appears in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2017, making the cited venue and year both incorrect with no matching publication found.

Lucia v. SEC is a real Supreme Court decision, but the citation contains metadata errors: the correct citation is 138 S. Ct. 2044 (2018), not 138 S. Ct. 1386 (2020). The case name uniquely identifies the real work despite the wrong page number and wrong year.

49 U.S.C. § 42121(a) is a confirmed, existing statute covering whistleblower protections for aviation employees under the AIR21 Act, verified at law.cornell.edu, FindLaw, and GovInfo. The citation specifies 'U.S.C.' as venue without a Title number, which is imprecise but the statute unambiguously exists in the U.S. Code.

No web evidence of any case named 'Nakashima v. Boeing Company' exists in any legal database or indexed source. Additionally, the page number 3568 within volume 842 of F. Supp. 3d is structurally impossible, as individual Federal Supplement volumes do not exceed roughly 1,500 pages, providing positive evidence of fabrication.

Searching for Rutter + Colling-Saltin + 1976 consistently returns the Springer article 'Ultrastructure of the small intestinal epithelium of the developing pig foetus' (DOI: 10.1007/BF00519037, Brain Structure and Function journal), which matches the described topic, authorship, and year. The cited title is a descriptive paraphrase of the real title.
The case Virginia House of Delegates v. Bethune-Hill is confirmed at 587 U.S. 658, decided by the Supreme Court on June 17, 2019. The case name, reporter volume and page, and year all match exactly.

Geoffrey H. Bourne was a real academic who published 'The Structure and Function of Muscle' in 1962, but no web evidence was found for a 1962 Bourne work titled 'The Structure and Function of the Small Intestine.' The title pattern matches his real series but with a different subject; however, absence of web evidence alone is insufficient to positively confirm non-existence for older academic books.

No UNFCCC document titled 'Review of the Kyoto Protocol' from 2005 was found across three web searches or in the UNFCCC document library. UNFCCC did publish review-related documents in 2005 (e.g., Article 8 guidelines at CMP 1), but none match this title; the citation may be fabricated or badly misattributed, but no positive evidence of non-existence was found.

The Doha Amendment to the Kyoto Protocol is a real 2012 UNFCCC instrument (decision 1/CMP.8), but no UNFCCC document titled 'Doha Amendment discussions and post-Kyoto reviews' exists in official UNFCCC archives or any indexed source. The cited title is a generic descriptive phrase with no matching official document, consistent with a hallucinated citation built around a real historical event.

Lecce and Morgan did publish in 1962, but their actual paper is 'Effect of dietary regimen on cessation of intestinal absorption of large molecules (closure) in the neonatal pig and lamb' in the Journal of Nutrition (78:263-268). The cited title 'Detailed ultrastructural observations of fetal pig intestinal epithelium development' does not match the real paper's subject matter and does not correspond to any identified publication by these authors.

The IPCC Fourth Assessment Report (AR4, 2007) and Fifth Assessment Report (AR5, 2014) are well-established, widely cited climate science publications from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Multiple authoritative sources including the IPCC's own archive and Wikipedia confirm their existence and details.

The book 'Section 504 and the ADA' by Russo and Osborne on Corwin Press is confirmed through multiple retailer listings. The citation has minor metadata errors: author order is swapped (Russo is actually listed first), year is off by one (2008 not 2007), and the subtitle may be a descriptive paraphrase rather than the official subtitle. None of these errors change which work is being cited.

The Journal of Race, Ethnicity and Politics Volume 5 (2020) table of contents on Cambridge Core contains no article by Persily or Egan, and the title 'The spaces between us: Race, distance, and political division in America' does not appear anywhere in the volume. The claimed page range (22-47) also does not correspond to any real article in that issue. The title appears to be a construct borrowing from Ryan Enos's real 2017 book 'The Space Between Us.'

Food Marketing Institute v. Argus Leader Media, 588 U.S. 427 (2019) is a real US Supreme Court decision. The Supreme Court's official preliminary print PDF confirms pages 427-444 of volume 588, and the case was decided June 24, 2019. All citation details are accurate.

The Restatement (Third) of Unfair Competition is a well-documented publication by the American Law Institute (1995), confirmed by the ALI's own website, LexisNexis catalog, WIPO Lex, and multiple law library databases. It is a recognized authoritative legal treatise cited by the U.S. Supreme Court.

Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization is a confirmed 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision. The cited reporter citation 142 S. Ct. 2228 is verified by multiple legal databases including vLex, which explicitly lists '142 S.Ct. 2228, 213 L.Ed.2d 545 (2022)'. All attribution elements match.

The book exists but was published in 2013 by University of Michigan Press (ISBNs 9780472119011, 9780472036578), not in 2020 by Oxford University Press. The DOI (10.1093/oso/9780190089268.001.0001) returns a 404 and appears fabricated to mimic an OUP scholarly monograph identifier. The citation describes a non-existent edition.

Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 113 (1973) is a well-documented U.S. Supreme Court case confirmed by Justia, the Library of Congress, and FindLaw with all citation details (case name, reporter citation, and year) fully matching.

No ERIC or Sage Journals record exists for this title attributed to Yell & Rozalski in Teaching Exceptional Children Vol. 40 (2008).
